Old English ǣfre Old English nǣfre Middle English nevere English never From Middle English nevere, navere, nævere, from Old English nǣfre (“never”), equivalent to ne + ever.

senses.d: At no time; on no occasion; in no circumstance.
ex: I finally finished, and I never do wanna do it again.
We were at the same college, but happened never to meet.

senses.d: Not at any other time; not on any other occasion; not previously.
ex:
1908, Lucy Maud Montgomery, Anne of Green Gables, Chapter XIII: The Delights of Anticipation,
I never saw such an infatuated man.
There is no jewel, be it of never so rich a price, which I set before this jewel: I mean your love.

senses.d: Negative particle (used to negate verbs in the simple past tense; also used absolutely).
ex: The police say I stole the car, but I never did it.
You said you were going to mow the lawn today. – I never!
That's what he said. But I never see anything. Maybe it's an invisible dog. Or very good at hiding.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French ja mais (“any more”, only in reference to the future), the two components deriving from Latin iam and magis. Compare Spanish jamás, Italian giammai, Occitan jamai and Portuguese jamais.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish nunqua, from Latin numquam, from ne + umquam.
Inherited from Old Spanish jamás, an early borrowing from Old Occitan ja mais. Compare Portuguese jamais and French jamais, Italian giammai.
From Old Galician-Portuguese nunca, from Latin numquam (“never”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese jamais, from Old Occitan ja mais, from Latin iam magis. Cognate with Galician xamais, Spanish jamás, Occitan jamai, French jamais and Italian giammai.

ety.text: From Middle English nevertheles, never-þe-les, nevere-þe-lesse. By surface analysis, never (“not at all”) + the + less; compare never the wiser.

senses.d: In spite of what preceded; yet.

ety.text: Univerbation of pour tant (“for so much”).

Inherited from Late Latin per hoc (“for this reason”, literally “through this”). The original meaning of però was “for this reason, therefore”. Cognate with Spanish pero, Old Franco-Provençal enperoi.
